rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding sūrah urges the Prophet to wait: persistent deniers receive only temporary respite under God's practice, and cannot escape His grasp.
rows.anchor: Sūrah al-Ṭāriq, the previous sūrah ended on urging the Prophet (sws) to show patience and to wait for the decision of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sūrah shifts its primary address from stubborn Quraysh to the Prophet and, over at least ten following sūrahs, dispels his preaching fears in varied ways.
rows.anchor: while ignoring these stubborn elements from among the Quraysh, the Prophet (sws) is addressed directly and given glad tidings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–5 direct the Prophet to glorify God, whose attributes show that creation and human physical and intellectual capacities mature gradually.
rows.anchor: based entirely on His wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–8 promise that revelation will mature for the Prophet, remain preserved except for what God wills to set aside, and bring ease from known hardships.
rows.anchor: The favour of revelations that he is receiving will gradually reach its culmination

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not pursue the obdurate or force the message: he is to remind when useful, while the fearful heed it and the wretched evade it and face their fate.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is directed not to go after the stubborn and the obdurate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fortunate attain success by purification, remembering their Lord, and prayer.
rows.anchor: Glad tidings of success are given to the fortunate who

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers prefer transient life to the better, eternal afterlife, so the Prophet's message finds no root in their hearts despite its continuity with earlier prophetic teaching.
rows.anchor: giving preference to this world over the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ means declaring the Almighty free of anything inconsistent with His majesty.
rows.anchor: serves to absolve the Almighty of all things which are against His majesty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True comprehension of God grounds knowledge, cognizance, power, and belief; errors in it lead to Satanic misguidance and weaken faith, trust, satisfaction, and perseverance.
rows.anchor: man is led away from true knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's remembrance comforts the heart, strengthens it, and keeps it content and on the right path.
rows.anchor: surely in the remembrance of God all hearts are comforted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer, especially tahajjud, is the highest form of tasbīḥ; continuous remembrance through daily routines sustains spiritual life and guards against Satan.
rows.anchor: is the prayer, especially the tahajjud prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is commanded to use tasbīḥ comprehensively as a source of fortitude and perseverance.
rows.anchor: to acquire fortitude and perseverance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's works and plans unfold gradually according to wisdom; people should patiently fulfill His directives, since delays are wise and hardships benefit them in both lives.
rows.anchor: all of Almighty’s works and plans are carried out in a gradual manner – a scheme which itself is totally based on His wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaqa can mean making a sketch or effigy as well as creating; the cited bird example illustrates that sense, while contextual taswiyah means perfecting.
rows.anchor: it also means “to make a sketch or an effigy of something.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human creation is not instantaneous: an initial sketch passes through stages until the person reaches completion; taswiyah can mean improving, flattening, or perfecting, and context selects perfection.
rows.anchor: after passing through many stages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God develops material and spiritual abilities, implants needs, and supplies the means and capacity to meet them, as in an infant guided to its mother's milk.
rows.anchor: if a child needs milk, then he has been provided with it through the bosoms of his mother

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse comprehensively covers moral awareness, prophetic guidance, and life's appointed trials: God's way leads to salvation, while deviation and whims lead to ruin.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has ingrained in him the awareness of good and evil and sent prophets and messengers to him for his guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word taswiyah can denote improving, flattening, or perfecting; the context chooses the sense of perfecting.
rows.anchor: here it is used in the last of these meanings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the common decay-based readings of black litter or waste: aḥwā describes reddish or greenish blackness produced by freshness, fertility, and luxuriant growth.
rows.anchor: because of freshness, fertility and luxuriance

rows.speaker: Ta’bbata Sharraṇ
rows.claim: The cited jāhili poet uses the description while praising a robust, healthy young man, supporting this fresh, vigorous sense of aḥwā.
rows.anchor: the famous poet of the jāhilliyah period, Ta’bbata Sharra ṇ, while extolling a person says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Through Imām al-Farāhī, the author cites Qaṭṭāmī's valley couplet depicting dense, layered undergrowth as evidence that ghuthāʾ can mean fertile luxuriant vegetation.
rows.anchor: he wrote while praising a valley

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because aḥwā does not denote decay-blackness and qualifies ghuthāʾ, the phrase means God brings out vegetation and makes it luxuriant and blackish green.
rows.anchor: makes them luxuriant and blackish green

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gradual law seen in human development and vegetation also governs the Prophet: his prophethood and revelation will mature, and he will overcome obstacles.
rows.anchor: The phases of his prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context matches the cautions against haste in Ṭāhā and al-Qiyāmah: revelation was the Prophet's needed support for opposition, future guidance, and answering objections, explaining his eagerness.
rows.anchor: The context and occasion of the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet eagerly repeated each word and wished to receive the whole revelation at once; God tells him not to hurry, since revelation follows a wise timetable.
rows.anchor: would be so enthusiastic at this instance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God guarantees the Qur'an's preservation so the Prophet will not forget; collection, recital, following, and explanation are all assigned to God.
rows.anchor: Indeed, upon Us is its collection and recital. So when We have recited it out, follow this recital. Then upon Us is to explain it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception for what God pleases concerns temporary directives later abrogated; God will tell the Prophet when their term ends.
rows.anchor: The reference is to the temporary directives which were later abrogated.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the Prophet's circumstances, worries, and prayers as well as his enemies' overt tricks and hidden plots; His knowledge and power ensure needed help.
rows.anchor: all his worries as well as his prayers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True faith and trust arise from firm awareness of God's all-embracing knowledge and all-encompassing power.
rows.anchor: true faith and trust in God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gives the Prophet clear glad tidings that present hardships will end and God will lead him toward ease.
rows.anchor: the hardships he is currently facing will one day end and the Almighty will lead him towards ease

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term rendered ease is described grammatically as an adjective modifying an implicit noun.
rows.anchor: is an adjective of a suppressed noun similar in meaning to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's hardships train and discipline him for future divine favor; this follows the law of gradual development, and ease comes after difficulty.
rows.anchor: The way ahead is clear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet need not be distressed or force the message: he should remind those inclined to hear and leave the others to their fate.
rows.anchor: His only responsibility is to remind others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses distinguish those who heed the warning from those who evade it; their rejection reflects their own condition, not a flaw in the message or preacher.
rows.anchor: the type of people who

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evaders treat this life as all that exists and fear no Hereafter; they face eternal Fire, neither living nor dying, and will wish in vain for death.
rows.anchor: They regard this life to be all that there is.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who preserve nature's God-given light recognize a prophet's call, or awaken when prompted; where that light is extinguished, only the Judgement trumpet can awaken them.
rows.anchor: people in whom this light has been totally extinguished

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The succeeding sūrah al-Ghāshiyah elaborates the same warning; its great torment and this passage's great Fire refer to the same punishment.
rows.anchor: Both refer to the same thing in slightly different styles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who benefited from the Prophet's reminders purify themselves from polytheism and disbelief and receive success and God's pleasure in both lives.
rows.anchor: receive the pleasure and blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God's name and praying are purification's foremost expression and method; prayer manifests belief, which grounds and guards the Sharīʿah's directives.
rows.anchor: manifestation of belief in the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh's hostility comes from attachment to worldly interests: they invent doubts rather than risk those interests for the Hereafter, sacrificing eternal reward for transient life.
rows.anchor: the Hereafter is more lasting and permanent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's teaching is not new: earlier revelation taught that the Hereafter is real life and each soul bears its own deeds and burden.
rows.anchor: whatever the Prophet (sws) is telling his addressees is not something new or unique

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' and Israelite prophets' scriptures survive in the Bible despite substantial alteration; they still clearly teach monotheism and the Hereafter and can revive faith.
rows.anchor: all of these very clearly and very effectively depict the teachings of monotheism and life in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham left oral exhortations rather than a scripture; his Israelite descendants preserved the teachings in writing, and their prophets renewed them, with evidence still present in scripture and the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: did not leave a scripture for the guidance of his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unlettered Ishmaelites preserved Abraham's teaching orally for a time, then lost it to neglect and innovations; Muhammad revived and completed it as God's enduring perfect religion.
rows.anchor: these teachings were not only revived, they were also completed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath sworn by horses is evidence for the later premise that man is ungrateful to his Lord.
rows.anchor: this oath sworn by the horses is a testimony to the ungratefulness of man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍabḥ is the sound from panting horses' nostrils; their exhausted state shows dutiful obedience and spending their last energy on their master's task.
rows.anchor: specific sound which comes out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-linked clauses are sequential and adjectives apply to the same noun; muwriyāt means producing fire and qadh striking, depicting iron-hoofed horses sparking as they gallop on stony ground.
rows.anchor: iron-clad strike the ground with such force

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dawn was the preferred time for Arabian raids; the alarm wa ṣabāḥā reflects this, and ṣabāḥ became a common term for plunder.
rows.anchor: the most appropriate to plunder an enemy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Athara means raising or inciting and naqʿ means dust.
rows.anchor: means “to make something rise” and “to incite”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If bihi refers to dawn, the assault raises a duststorm over the enemy; if it refers to the first verse's gallop, that gallop generates dust. Both portray a whirlwind attack.
rows.anchor: when they raid the enemy they raise a storm of dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bā indicates association and the pronoun refers to dust: the horses pierce the enemy crowd without fearing weapons, valuing their masters' mission above their lives.
rows.anchor: not fearing their spears and swords to the slightest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kanūd means ungrateful: a person who witnesses horses' obedience and benefits from their sacrifice yet ignores his own duty to God is more ungrateful than animals that know a master's rights.
rows.anchor: an ungrateful person who does not value the favours of his Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Horses exemplify service found throughout animals God placed at man's disposal; Qur'anic mentions, especially of camels, should awaken gratitude and teach submission, diligence, and patience.
rows.anchor: camels are mentioned at numerous places

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Horses are singled out because clans needed high-pedigree warhorses for attack, defense, and family protection; their importance also made them common in classical poetry.
rows.anchor: they had great importance in launching an onslaught on the enemy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author cites a Ḥamāsī poet's verse about spending on a thoroughbred horse as a house sentinel and keeping a servant for it, illustrating horses' esteem.
rows.anchor: I am restricting myself to just one couplet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People understand a servant's value from its service, yet man disobeys his Lord and still expects the greatest afterlife reward; horses serve only because God subjected them to man.
rows.anchor: the real value of a servant depends on his services

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike horses, man remains indifferent to worshipping and serving the Creator who made him, all useful animals, and every means of his sustenance.
rows.anchor: all other animals who are of use to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man needs no outside proof of his ingratitude: he himself witnesses it, as in al-Qiyāmah's declaration that a person testifies against himself despite excuses.
rows.anchor: man himself is a witness upon his own self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nature and conscience testify to obvious moral truths; people evade them because they conflict with base desires, not because evidence is lacking, and rationalize unjust expectations from God.
rows.anchor: obvious requisites of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khayr here means wealth; man hoards blessings as his own achievement, unlike the obedient horse that returns its spoils and accepts its master's feed, while boasting as in Qārūn's claim.
rows.anchor: whatever favours man is blessed with by the Almighty are regarded by him to be the result of his own planning and skill

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God, man's creator and benefactor, is truly worthy of love; believers prefer Him when self-interest conflicts, while the ungrateful cherish wealth more than their Lord.
rows.anchor: the believers are the most stern in their love for God
